core: What makes a source secondary: created later, one step removed from the events, and analyzing/interpreting/summarizing primary evidence
Typical secondary sources: textbooks, scholarly books and journal articles, documentaries, biographies written after the fact
Why the SAME item can be primary or secondary depending on the research question
Scholarly standards (peer review, full citation) and how to judge a secondary source's reliability
Historiography: how historians build on and argue with earlier scholarship

Corroboration and evaluating author, intent, and context

claims.claim: A secondary source is an account created after the events it describes—one step removed from them—that interprets, analyzes, or summarizes primary evidence.
Common secondary sources include textbooks, scholarly monographs, peer-reviewed journal articles, biographies written after the fact, documentaries, dissertations, and reviews.

Whether an item is a primary or a secondary source depends on the research question: e.g., a textbook is a secondary source for its own subject but a primary source for a study of how textbooks (or a field's ideas) changed over time.

Scholarly secondary sources are vetted by standards such as peer review and full citation of evidence; markers of reliability include author expertise, a university press or recognized scholarly publisher, cited references, and appropriate currency.

Historiography is the study of how historians have interpreted a topic over time; scholars are in conversation, building on and disputing earlier work as they interpret, analyze, and synthesize primary sources and the research of other historians.
Historians who examine the same evidence can reach different conclusions because secondary work involves interpretation shaped by the scholar's questions, methods, and context.
When evaluating any source, historians examine the author, audience, intent, and context, and corroborate it against other sources and scholarship.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Some reference works (encyclopedias) are labeled 'secondary' by some guides and 'tertiary' by others.
positions: UMass Boston lists encyclopedias among secondary sources
Other library frameworks call encyclopedias and textbooks 'tertiary' sources that compile secondary work
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson treats the primary/secondary line as the core distinction and notes that some frameworks add a 'tertiary' category for reference compilations; it does not overstate a single fixed taxonomy.

sourceRecords.title: World History, Volume 1, Section 1.2: Primary Sources
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed OER survey. Defines primary sources as coming directly from the period and secondary sources as written/created after the fact; frames evaluating sources by author, audience, intent, and context, and corroboration against other scholars. Used to support the primary/secondary contrast and source-evaluation claims. Prose written original to avoid NC/SA reuse constraints.

sourceRecords.title: Primary Sources: A Research Guide — Primary vs. Secondary
sourceRecords.provider: University of Massachusetts Boston, Healey Library
sourceRecords.notes: University library guide. States secondary sources are 'one step removed from primary sources' and add interpretation/analysis; lists books, articles, documentaries, biographies, dissertations, reviews as examples; explicitly gives the context-dependent case that a textbook is secondary for its field but primary for a study of the history of textbooks / science education. No reuse license shown; REFERENCE_ONLY.

sourceRecords.title: History Resources at the UTM Library — Primary vs. Secondary Sources
sourceRecords.notes: University library guide. Defines secondary sources as works written after events that explain/interpret/analyze/judge past events (e.g., scholarly books and editorial analyses of primary collections). Discusses peer review (referee process), and reliability markers: cited references, a university press or recognized scholarly publisher, and scholarly article structure. Supports the scholarly-standards/reliability claim. No reuse license shown; REFERENCE_ONLY.

sourceRecords.title: Write a Historiography — Research Guide
sourceRecords.notes: University library guide on historiography. Describes secondary sources as texts containing research by historians who analyzed primary sources, and explains that scholars using the same records can reach very different conclusions and are in conversation—building on and disputing earlier work, interpreting, analyzing, and synthesizing prior scholarship. Supports the historiography and differing-interpretation claims. No reuse license shown; REFERENCE_ONLY.
